04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The reference to an authorisation register had looked promising when Fiona first mentioned it. By morning it had become another problem of incomplete records. The September 2011 delegated-authority sheet named roles and responsibilities, but no verified approver; the register that might contain actual decisions had not been located.

Fiona called with the results of a further search. A storage inventory prepared in 2012 referred to an approvals book for the student travel scheme and assigned it a box number. That numbered box was not among those currently kept in the trust's principal store.

“Then it was removed,” Sarah said when Emma told her.

“Possibly moved, yes. But removed deliberately? We have no evidence of that.”

Fiona was equally cautious. The box might have been transferred, reorganised or recorded incorrectly. No destruction notice had been found, which did not guarantee that the material survived. She offered to check other inventories without revealing applicants' personal information.

Emma compared the new reference with the delegated-authority procedure. It distinguished requests for exceptions from approvals and required cases above a threshold to be referred to the trust chair. The threshold figure remained illegible. Malcolm Vale's position as chair did not establish that he had signed any particular authorisation, still less that a payment had been executed.

Sarah wanted to connect the book with Helen Ward's cousin, whose redacted letter described a selected application. Emma refused. There was still no verified transfer, and nothing tied that application to an exception, an approval or the missing register.

In the afternoon Fiona forwarded a further description, this time from a transfer list for an external storage provider. It contained the same box reference. The provider's name was faint, and the paperwork did not confirm receipt of the box.

“Now we have a chain,” Sarah said.

“A possible chain,” Emma replied. “A line on a transfer list is not a signed delivery record.”

The distinction mattered. If a box had reached an outside warehouse, it might still be retrievable. If it had been mislabelled or never collected, looking there could lead nowhere. Neither scenario, on its own, suggested interference with the trust's accounts.

Emma wrote three questions for Fiona: could the provider be identified, was there a receipt or tracking number, and did a later inventory mention the box? She asked for descriptions, not the names of students or recipients.

As she saved the notes, she heard the anonymous caller's instruction again: ask who approved the payments. That question was unchanged. The route to answering it had become unexpectedly physical: a possible book, a numbered carton and an uncertain journey into storage.

For the moment, she could report only that a historical inventory referred to a register whose whereabouts were unknown.
